text: Fourteen years on, I went up to Jerusalem again, this time with Barnabas, bringing Titus along too.
I went because of a revelation, and I laid out privately, before the recognized leaders, the message I preach among the nations — not wanting my work to have run for nothing.
And Titus, who was with me, a Greek, wasn't made to be circumcised.
That pressure came from infiltrators who slipped in to spy on the freedom we have in Christ, hoping to drag us back into bondage.
We didn't yield to them for a moment, so that the true message of the good news would remain intact for you.
As for the ones who seemed important — whatever they were makes no difference to me, God plays no favorites — those leaders added nothing to what I preach.
Quite the opposite: they saw I'd been entrusted with the message for the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been for the circumcised.
The same God who worked through Peter's mission to the circumcised worked through mine to the nations.
So James, Cephas, and John, regarded as pillars there, recognized the grace given me and shook hands with Barnabas and me in agreement — we'd go to the nations, they to the circumcised.
Their only request was that we keep remembering the poor, which I was already eager to do.
But when Cephas came to Antioch, I confronted him directly, because he was clearly in the wrong.
Before certain men arrived from James, he used to eat with the Gentile believers; once they showed up, he pulled back and kept his distance, afraid of the circumcision faction.
The rest of the Jewish believers joined his pretense, and even Barnabas got swept into it.

Seeing they weren't walking straight with the truth of the message, I said to Cephas in front of everyone: if you, a Jew, live like the Gentiles rather than like a Jew, why are you pressuring the Gentiles to live like Jews?
We who are Jews by birth, not sinners from the nations —

still know that no one is made right with God by keeping the law, but only through faith in Jesus Christ. So we too put our trust in Christ Jesus, to be made right by faith in him, not by law-keeping — because no one is made right by the law.
And if, in seeking to be made right in Christ, we ourselves turn out to be sinners, does that make Christ a promoter of sin? Certainly not.
If I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself a lawbreaker.
Through the law itself I died to the law, so that I might live for God.
I've been crucified with Christ; it's no longer I who live, but Christ living in me. The life I live now in this body I live by trusting the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
I won't set aside God's grace — for if being right with God came through the law, then Christ died for no reason.
